paragraphs: Any3D-VLA investigates how three-dimensional visual information can improve models that translate images and language into robot actions. Images alone can make spatial relationships difficult to interpret in complex scenes. The authors first compare observation spaces and visual representations, finding that explicitly converting visual input into point clouds produces information that complements the corresponding two-dimensional representations.

The proposed training pipeline brings together point clouds from simulators, physical sensors, and model-based estimates. This diversity addresses two related problems: limited availability of 3D training data and differences between environments or depth scales. The model learns 3D representations intended to remain useful across those differences, then combines them with matching 2D representations.

Experiments in simulation and the real world report improved performance and a smaller domain gap. The contribution therefore concerns both adding spatial information and making that information usable across varied sources. The findings support training with diverse point clouds as a way to strengthen VLA robustness while retaining complementary information from ordinary images.
icml-2026-any3d-vla-enhancing-vla-robust.tldr: Any3D-VLA combines images with diverse point clouds to improve robot performance and reduce differences across environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a small language model running on a device can decide when to ask a more capable cloud model for help. A separate router usually makes that decision from the incoming prompt, but the authors argue that prompt inspection can miss the difficulty of complex reasoning. They instead train the local model to make the decision internally.

Reinforcement learning supplies hierarchical rewards that encourage both local problem solving and selective cloud use. The training algorithm includes a group-level policy gradient to stabilize optimization. It also filters prompts adaptively to provide complementary learning signals, addressing the risk that the model settles into always answering locally or always requesting cloud assistance.

Experiments use device-scale LLaMA and Qwen models across several reasoning benchmarks. The method consistently improves over the evaluated baselines and substantially reduces the performance gap to full cloud models. The results support treating assistance requests as a learned part of reasoning, with training explicitly balancing the two available execution choices.
icml-2026-bridging-on-device-and-cloud-l.tldr: Reinforcement learning teaches on-device language models to solve queries locally or selectively request cloud assistance.

paragraphs: De4D-SLAM tackles camera tracking and scene reconstruction from a single camera when objects can move. Conventional methods often discard moving objects using predefined categories, leaving parts of the environment poorly represented. Gaussian scene representations can include both stationary and moving content, but their flexible moving components can also fit errors that actually belong to the static scene.

That unwanted fitting removes the reconstruction errors needed to identify genuine motion. De4D-SLAM separates the relevant gradient signals so static reconstruction residuals can supervise a spatially aware Kolmogorov-Arnold network for motion segmentation. This allows motion detection without relying on object categories. A second component uses dense optical flow to initialize the changing Gaussian representation and stabilize its difficult optimization.

Evaluations on TUM and Bonn report competitive camera tracking and dynamic reconstruction. These findings support the framework’s effort to preserve reliable localization while also reconstructing a scene that changes over time. Its central contribution is managing how static and dynamic components learn, so their flexibility does not destroy the evidence used to distinguish them.
icml-2026-de4d-slam-gradient-isolated-st.tldr: De4D-SLAM separates static and dynamic learning signals to support camera tracking and changing-scene reconstruction without object-category priors.

paragraphs: This paper examines deception in models that process both images and text. It distinguishes strategically misleading answers, given correct internal representations, from hallucinations caused by limited capability. The authors introduce MM-DeceptionBench to study such behavior across six realistic categories, extending an evaluation problem previously investigated mainly in text-only settings.

The authors find that text-centered monitoring does not adequately handle the cross-modal reasoning involved. Their proposed evaluation framework, debate with images, uses multiple agents in adversarial debate while requiring arguments to remain grounded in visual evidence. The intended benefit is to make image content part of the scrutiny applied to a potentially misleading response.

In experiments involving GPT-4o, the framework agrees more closely with human judgments than the evaluated MLLM-as-a-judge baselines. The reported gains reach 1.5 times the Cohen’s kappa score and 1.25 times the accuracy. These are improvements in detecting and evaluating deceptive behavior; they support visually grounded debate as a monitoring approach rather than establishing that the underlying models stop producing deception.
icml-2026-debate-with-images-detecting-d.tldr: A multimodal deception benchmark and visually grounded debate framework improve agreement with human judgments of deceptive model behavior.

paragraphs: Event2Vec addresses the mismatch between event cameras and conventional deep learning pipelines. These cameras provide sparse, asynchronous observations with strong temporal resolution, power efficiency, and dynamic range. Converting events into dense frames loses their original sparse timing structure, while models designed for irregular data can be less compatible with GPU acceleration.

Inspired by word-to-vector representations, the paper introduces a vector representation that lets Transformers process events directly. The key idea is to make the event format usable within a high-throughput architecture while retaining direct access to event data. This connects the camera’s unusual output format to a model family suited to efficient computation.

Evaluations on DVS Gesture, ASL-DVS, and DVS-Lip report parameter efficiency, high throughput, and low latency. The method also achieves high accuracy when only very few events or low spatial resolutions are available. Together, these findings support direct event representations as a practical route toward efficient neuromorphic vision, including settings where the available visual observations are especially sparse.
icml-2026-event2vec-processing-neuromorp.tldr: Event2Vec represents camera events directly as vectors, enabling efficient Transformer processing even with sparse or low-resolution observations.

paragraphs: FSLoRA studies collaborative language-model fine-tuning when participating clients have different computational and communication resources. Low-rank adaptation reduces the size of the trainable update, but its rank still creates a trade-off: higher ranks generally improve performance while requiring more resources. A shared training system must therefore accommodate clients that cannot all support the same update size.

The framework maintains global LoRA modules on a server and lets clients selectively update submatrices through a sketching mechanism. Each client’s sketching ratio determines the rank of its local submatrix. Adjusting that ratio makes the amount of local work responsive to the client’s capabilities while keeping its updates connected to the server’s global modules.

The paper provides a convergence analysis that explicitly relates sketching ratios to convergence rate. Experiments report better performance than the evaluated baselines and improved training efficiency with stable convergence. The contribution is a resource-adaptive update mechanism accompanied by analysis of how its central control parameter affects learning, rather than only an empirical recipe for heterogeneous clients.
icml-2026-federated-sketching-lora-a-fle.tldr: FSLoRA lets clients update differently sized portions of shared LoRA modules to accommodate unequal resources in federated fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Human preference feedback can reflect who gets recruited or exposed to a system, rather than the population weighting its designer intends. This paper models annotators sampled through a network. It shows that a scalar reward model ignoring annotator identity implicitly aggregates preferences according to inclusion probabilities, potentially giving structurally central communities excessive influence when those probabilities differ from the target weighting.

Graph-Preference Learning combines personalized reward predictions with balanced aggregation. Neighboring annotators share statistical information, while stabilized importance weights adjust how their predictions contribute to the aggregate. The analysis bounds the difference from the intended welfare in terms of weighting mismatch, reward-model approximation, and finite-sample effects.

Experiments use synthetic graphs and an LMArena case study with deliberately induced graph-based sampling bias. They report up to 62% lower target-welfare recovery error and 17% smaller cross-language performance gaps under biased inclusion. The semi-synthetic design matters: these findings demonstrate correction of the constructed sampling bias, rather than establishing that the original dataset was collected through that same process.
icml-2026-graph-preference-learning-debi.tldr: Graph-Preference Learning adjusts network-sampled feedback so aggregate rewards better reflect a designer’s intended population weighting.

paragraphs: Immuno-VLM addresses a failure mode in recognizing unfamiliar visual inputs: broad semantic similarity can cause a model to assign an unknown anomaly to a familiar category with high confidence. The authors connect this behavior to a lack of explicit negative knowledge. Knowing what belongs to a category does not itself provide descriptions of nearby cases that should be excluded.

The framework takes inspiration from biological negative selection. It uses a language model’s generative reasoning to create textual descriptions of near-distribution outliers, such as look-alikes and contextual anomalies. These descriptions, called semantic antibodies, help bound known classes in the latent representation space without requiring outlier images to be generated in pixel space.

Experiments on ImageNet-1K and four out-of-distribution benchmarks report state-of-the-art results. The stated findings support actively constructing semantic counterexamples as a way to improve recognition of unfamiliar inputs. The distinctive contribution is using generated negative descriptions to refine category boundaries, addressing the same broad semantic abstraction that makes vision-language models useful for zero-shot recognition.
icml-2026-immuno-vlm-immunizing-large-vi.tldr: Immuno-VLM generates textual descriptions of plausible outliers to help vision-language models distinguish unknown anomalies from familiar categories.

paragraphs: InfoGeo Loss treats forecasting as learning distributions over future observations. The paper argues that pointwise Euclidean errors overlook the geometry of those distributions, making predicted and true distributions harder to align, especially for uncertainty quantification. Its proposed loss therefore evaluates discrepancies using the structure of the statistical space in which the distributions live.

The method combines three components. A parameterization module represents predictions through learnable sufficient statistics. A Fisher information metric measures intrinsic distributional distance, while a Bregman divergence accounts for asymmetric prediction errors. A natural-gradient weighting strategy supports efficient optimization within this geometry, connecting the representation of a forecast to the way its errors influence learning.

The authors prove statistical consistency and provide convergence guarantees within their theoretical treatment. Experiments spanning seven datasets and five architectures report consistent improvements over existing losses, averaging 6.8% in MSE and 5.3% in MAE. These results indicate that a distribution-oriented training objective can also improve the conventional pointwise forecasting metrics used in the evaluation.
icml-2026-information-geometry-loss-for-.tldr: InfoGeo Loss uses probability-distribution geometry to train forecasters, improving average MSE and MAE across the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: iWorld-Bench evaluates world models as interactive environments, with attention to abilities such as distance perception and memory. The motivation is that agents need environments supporting perception, reasoning, and action, while existing evaluation resources do not adequately cover physical interaction. The benchmark organizes evaluation around several capabilities that matter when generated worlds must respond to actions.

The authors construct a dataset of 330,000 video clips and select 2,100 high-quality samples spanning different perspectives, weather conditions, and scenes. Because world models accept different interaction modalities, they introduce a common Action Generation Framework. It supports six task types and produces 4,900 test samples assessing visual generation, trajectory following, and memory.

The study evaluates 14 representative world models and reports identifying limitations that can inform subsequent research. The benchmark’s contribution is a shared way to examine multiple aspects of interaction across otherwise differing systems. Its combination of tasks makes visual quality one part of evaluation alongside following an action trajectory and retaining relevant information.
icml-2026-iworld-bench-a-benchmark-for-i.tldr: iWorld-Bench provides unified tasks for comparing interactive world models on visual generation, trajectory following, and memory.

paragraphs: LOZO+ targets memory-efficient language-model fine-tuning through zeroth-order optimization, which estimates useful update directions from loss feedback. Earlier low-rank approaches sample random subspaces with a fixed rank. Although this matches the idea that language-model gradients have low-rank structure, random sampling does not guarantee alignment with the directions that dominate the actual gradient.

The proposed method uses loss feedback to assess candidate directions and greedily select a low-rank subspace. An adaptive threshold retains directions that produce substantial descent. This makes subspace selection responsive to the optimization problem: the algorithm uses observed progress to decide which directions deserve a place in subsequent updates.

The paper develops a convergence framework and proves superiority over existing methods within that analysis. Experiments consistently outperform the evaluated zeroth-order approaches and achieve performance competitive with a first-order algorithm while retaining zeroth-order memory efficiency. The central finding is that choosing low-rank directions deliberately can be more effective than relying on the low-rank format alone.
icml-2026-lozo-provably-efficient-zeroth.tldr: LOZO+ uses loss feedback to select productive low-rank update directions for memory-efficient language-model fine-tuning.

paragraphs: MC-HNN studies how hypergraph neural networks represent high-order relationships. In the common two-stage design, node information travels through hyperedges before contributing to node updates. The paper identifies two structural bottlenecks in this process: rank collapse and hyperedge semantic dependency. These concern the diversity of the learned representations and the independence of the information represented by hyperedges.

The proposed network addresses the two bottlenecks with separate mechanisms. Multiple message-passing channels are designed to maintain high-rank representations, preserving a richer set of representational directions. A latent hyperedge type encoding adds an independent degree of freedom to hyperedge representations, allowing their learned semantics to carry information beyond the dependency identified in the standard design.

The authors’ analysis and experiments suggest that these changes alleviate the bottlenecks and produce strong empirical performance. That qualification is part of the finding: the paper presents support for reducing these structural problems. Its contribution links two diagnosed limitations to targeted architectural changes, rather than treating improved predictive performance as the only evidence of a better representation.
icml-2026-mc-hnn-learning-latent-structu.tldr: MC-HNN combines multiple message-passing channels with latent hyperedge types to alleviate two representation bottlenecks in hypergraph networks.

paragraphs: MINT studies how an AI planning partner should ask people for information when objects, goals, or intentions are unknown. Its focus is the effect of missing knowledge on planning outcomes. An effective interaction strategy must decide which human inputs are valuable enough to request, rather than treating every unresolved detail as equally relevant to the task.

The method builds a symbolic tree of possible human-AI interactions and consults a neural planning policy to estimate uncertainty caused by remaining knowledge gaps. Self-play helps optimize elicitation strategies. A language model then searches and summarizes the tree’s reasoning to curate questions intended to improve planning performance.

The paper analyzes a return guarantee for a given MINT within a family of extended Markov decision processes that include knowledge gaps and human elicitation. Across three benchmarks involving increasingly realistic unknown or unseen objects, MINT-based planning achieves near-expert returns with limited questions per task. Reported reward and success-rate improvements support connecting question selection directly to the consequences of missing information for planning.
icml-2026-mint-minimal-information-neuro.tldr: MINT combines symbolic interaction trees and neural planning to ask targeted human questions that improve plans with limited information.

paragraphs: NAVIGATE tests whether a vision-language model can decide when web search is needed and how to direct it from visual evidence. The problem becomes difficult when images contain ambiguous, overlapping, or conflicting clues. A model must work out what the images imply before it can choose useful search directions and revise them as reasoning progresses.

The benchmark contains 500 questions across 20 domains and three difficulty tiers. Tasks range from self-contained questions about one image to joint searches across multiple images and problems combining domains. Search targets are not supplied explicitly, so the evaluation includes deciding whether outside information is necessary as well as planning the search itself.

Across the evaluated models and search-enabled systems, performance remains low; Gemini-3-Pro-Preview-Search achieves 36.4% accuracy. The authors identify persistent problems in connecting evidence across images, triggering searches, and coordinating search strategies. These findings show that access to a search tool leaves substantial challenges in deciding how to use it when the starting evidence is visual.
icml-2026-navigate-evaluating-visual-gui.tldr: NAVIGATE reveals substantial difficulty in deciding when and how to search the web from ambiguous visual evidence.

paragraphs: SAFT addresses how strongly fine-tuning should push a language model toward target tokens it currently considers unlikely. Standard negative log-likelihood can apply disproportionately aggressive updates to these tokens, encouraging sensitivity to difficult examples and unwarranted confidence. The paper argues that alternatives such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning can move too far in the other direction, weakening gradients needed to learn new concepts.

Spectrum-Adaptive Fine-Tuning interpolates between the strong learning signal of negative log-likelihood and probability-weighted optimization. Its adaptive balance aims to reduce sensitivity to outliers while keeping updates effective enough for learning. The contribution is therefore a way to manage competing properties of the training objective through one unified framework.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and improved generalization to out-of-distribution tasks. Evaluations of general conversational alignment also support applicability across different data regimes. Together, these findings suggest that adjusting the strength of learning signals can improve both reasoning and broader alignment, while addressing the specific tension between aggressive fitting and insufficient learning.
icml-2026-navigating-the-pareto-frontier.tldr: SAFT adaptively balances strong and probability-weighted learning signals to improve fine-tuning robustness without sacrificing learning efficiency.

paragraphs: NExT-Guard addresses safety monitoring when a language model streams its response before the entire answer is available. A safeguard that checks only completed responses cannot intervene at the moment unsafe content appears. Training a separate streaming monitor with token-level labels is one option, but the paper identifies annotation expense and severe overfitting as problems with that approach.

The authors argue that well-trained post-hoc safeguards already contain token-level risk signals in their hidden representations. NExT-Guard accesses interpretable latent features using sparse autoencoders and monitors those features during streaming. It uses pretrained autoencoders from publicly available base language models, avoiding the need for token-level supervision.

Experiments report stronger performance than the evaluated post-hoc and supervised streaming safeguards, with robustness across models, autoencoder variants, and risk scenarios. These findings support reusing internal representations for real-time monitoring. The practical significance is that an existing safeguard’s learned information can support earlier intervention without requiring a new dataset labeling risk at every token.
icml-2026-next-guard-streaming-safeguard.tldr: NExT-Guard uses sparse-autoencoder features to monitor streaming safety without token-level training labels.

paragraphs: OMP adapts single-step MeanFlow generation to robot manipulation. Generative robot policies face an efficiency challenge: diffusion models can require costly inference, while flow-based alternatives often involve complex architectural constraints. The authors identify spectral bias and weak learning signals in low-velocity regimes as obstacles to directly transferring MeanFlow from image generation to robotics.

The method adds a lightweight directional-alignment mechanism that brings predicted velocities into agreement with true mean velocities. It also introduces a Differential Derivation Equation to approximate the Jacobian-vector product used in the method. This approximation separates forward and backward passes, substantially reducing memory complexity while supporting the proposed training approach.

Experiments on Adroit and Meta-World report better success rates and trajectory accuracy than the evaluated state-of-the-art methods, especially for high-precision tasks. OMP retains single-step generation in these evaluations. The results support the paper’s aim of combining precise manipulation with efficient inference, while its two technical components address velocity learning and memory costs within the same framework.
icml-2026-omp-one-step-meanflow-policy-w.tldr: OMP improves single-step robot action generation through velocity-direction alignment and a memory-efficient derivative approximation.

paragraphs: Programming-by-example asks a model to infer a program from a small collection of input-output pairs. The paper focuses on complex cases where language models misunderstand the behavior those examples imply. The resulting program may satisfy only some examples or follow an entirely different rule. The proposed approach gives feedback during synthesis to improve that interpretation process.

The authors first construct reasoning trees to create a dataset for process supervision. They then train a process reward model through preference learning so it can assess the effectiveness of individual reasoning steps. Finally, a curriculum organized by task difficulty guides reinforcement learning with Proximal Policy Optimization.

On representative programming-by-example benchmarks, the method reaches an average pass rate of 56.61%, with a reported 8.73% improvement over the state-of-the-art baseline. These findings support evaluating intermediate reasoning as a useful training signal for program synthesis. The approach ties that feedback to a difficulty-based curriculum, helping train the model to capture the intended behavior expressed by examples.
icml-2026-prm-pbe-process-reward-model-f.tldr: PRM-PBE uses step-level rewards and a difficulty-based curriculum to improve program synthesis from input-output examples.

paragraphs: This paper rethinks how models fill missing observations in time series. The authors argue that reconstructing missing values from limited context restricts the flow of temporal information and does not explicitly describe how the series evolves. Their Conditional Temporal Inference Paradigm instead treats imputation as inference conditioned on that temporal evolution.

The accompanying model, CBiT, compresses long-range history into a compact latent representation. That representation conditions the estimation of missing values, giving the model a way to use historical information beyond a narrow local context. A partitioned modeling strategy treats historical context and the imputation targets separately while maintaining linear-time complexity.

Experiments on multiple public benchmarks report reductions of 27.3% in Masked MAE and 18.6% in Masked RMSE across different missing rates. These measures assess error on the missing entries being reconstructed. The findings support combining explicit temporal inference with compressed history as an effective imputation strategy, with the partitioned design providing a computationally efficient way to organize the task.
icml-2026-rethinking-time-series-imputat.tldr: CBiT fills missing time-series values using compressed long-range history and temporal inference with linear-time complexity.

paragraphs: SLAP addresses the temporal gaps created when video-language models inspect only sparsely sampled frames. Important transitions can occur between those frames, leaving the model without evidence of how events connect. The authors argue that generative interpolation and autoregressive extrapolation can lose semantic consistency over long intervals, including allowing represented objects to disappear.

Their approach describes the video’s latent trajectory using a mathematical correspondence with classical mechanics. The trajectory lies on a Riemannian manifold and is governed by a semantic Lagrangian. Interpolation becomes a boundary-value problem: the observed endpoints constrain an intervening path, which is solved using discrete Euler-Lagrange equations.

This formulation enforces object persistence in the latent representation without rendering intermediate pixels. Experiments on multiple challenging datasets report that the approach is effective. The contribution is a structured way to connect sparse observations through semantic dynamics, making consistency of the intervening trajectory part of the interpolation problem itself rather than relying solely on generated intermediate content.
icml-2026-slap-the-semantic-least-action.tldr: SLAP uses a mechanics-inspired boundary-value formulation to connect sparse video frames while preserving objects in latent space.

paragraphs: TRACE studies causal systems whose mechanisms change gradually over time. The paper contrasts this setting with temporal causal representation methods that assume instantaneous switches between discrete domains. A gradual turn or transition in gait motivates a model that can represent intermediate mechanisms, rather than assigning every moment to one sharply separated regime.

The authors assume transitional mechanisms can be expressed as convex combinations of finitely many atomic mechanisms, with mixing coefficients that vary over time. Within this formulation, their theory establishes joint identifiability of the latent causal variables and the mixing trajectory. TRACE implements the idea through a mixture of experts, with each expert learning an atomic mechanism.

At test time, the framework recovers mechanism trajectories, including intermediate states absent from training. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report trajectory correlations reaching 0.99 and substantially better results than discrete-switching baselines. The findings support recovering continuous change through learned component mechanisms, with the convex-mixture formulation providing the structure behind the theoretical and empirical results.
icml-2026-trace-trajectory-recovery-for-.tldr: TRACE models gradual causal changes as time-varying mixtures of atomic mechanisms and recovers their continuous trajectories.

paragraphs: This paper converts Diffusion Transformers into spiking neural networks to improve energy efficiency without retraining. The central obstacle is that activation ranges change substantially across the iterative denoising process. Fixed-scale spiking neurons cannot accommodate those changes well, and the resulting conversion errors accumulate across steps, degrading the quality of generated images.

The proposed framework combines multi-threshold neurons with membrane-potential error feedback. Multiple firing levels let discrete spikes express a richer range of values. The feedback mechanism reuses residual membrane potential across successive denoising steps, exploiting their temporal correlation to compensate for lost information and reduce the effect of shifting activation distributions.

ImageNet experiments report competitive generative quality alongside superior energy efficiency, establishing a new reported benchmark for spiking Diffusion Transformers. The contribution is specifically trajectory-aware conversion: it uses information carried between denoising steps to manage error. This connects the iterative structure responsible for diffusion’s computational expense to a mechanism that helps preserve quality in the converted spiking network.
icml-2026-trajectory-aware-spiking-dits-.tldr: Multi-threshold spikes and cross-step membrane feedback improve energy-efficient Diffusion Transformer conversion without retraining.

paragraphs: This paper asks which parts of a long reasoning trace should guide a student model’s training. Standard supervised fine-tuning gives every token equal treatment, including redundant, noisy, or example-specific steps. The authors argue that this can encourage imitation of superficial patterns instead of transferable reasoning, motivating an analysis of the parameter updates associated with different steps.

Their Loss Subspace Attribution analysis decomposes gradients and finds that effective reasoning signals predominantly occupy a low-rank consensus subspace. Conflicting or unstructured signals dominate the remaining subspace. Spectral-guided Learning uses this structure to prioritize reasoning steps aligned with the consensus directions and suppress contributions from the residual directions.

Across several large reasoning models and diverse complex reasoning tasks, experiments consistently report more robust and generalizable students. The result supports selecting training influence according to shared gradient structure. The finding is about where useful signals predominantly concentrate; the method turns that observed geometric pattern into a step-level distillation strategy rather than uniformly fitting every part of a long trace.
icml-2026-uncovering-the-gradient-geomet.tldr: Spectral-guided Learning prioritizes reasoning steps whose gradients align with shared low-rank directions, improving student-model robustness and generalization.

paragraphs: XR-1 addresses two challenges in robot vision-language-action models: translating rich observations into precise actions and learning across heterogeneous data sources. Different robots and human demonstrations provide complementary information, but their differences make joint learning difficult. The paper introduces a shared intermediate representation intended to connect visual changes with robot motion.

Unified Vision-Motion Codes are discrete latent codes learned by a dual-branch vector-quantized autoencoder. They jointly encode visual dynamics and robotic motion, bridging observations and actions while aligning dynamic information across sources. Training proceeds through self-supervised code learning, code-guided pretraining on large cross-embodiment robot datasets, and task-specific post-training.

The evaluation includes more than 12,000 real-world rollouts on six robot embodiments and over 120 manipulation tasks. XR-1 consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines, including π₀ and GR00T-N1.5, and shows strong generalization to new objects, background changes, distractors, and lighting changes. These findings support joint vision-motion representations as a way to make heterogeneous robot experience useful for both precise control and broader generalization.
icml-2026-xr-1-towards-versatile-vision-.tldr: XR-1 learns shared discrete vision-motion codes to improve robot control and generalization across diverse embodiments and tasks.

paragraphs: ZeroDiff reconstructs a target time series at locations where that target has never been measured. The setting assumes that external input variables are available even though target observations are missing. Training can use measured locations, but the model must transfer what it learns to locations without their own target history.

A direct mapping from external inputs to target values can produce overly smooth series and underestimate extremes because it fails to capture the target’s intrinsic dynamics. ZeroDiff first constructs an informed prior using only the external variables. It then learns, through diffusion, to calibrate reconstruction errors using data from observed locations.

Experiments on diverse real-world datasets report significant improvements over existing approaches. The findings support explicitly learning corrections to an externally informed reconstruction, rather than relying only on the initial mapping. Here, zero-shot reconstruction refers to the absence of target measurements at the destination locations; the method still learns its calibration behavior from locations where target observations are available.
icml-2026-zerodiff-zero-shot-time-series.tldr: ZeroDiff learns diffusion-based corrections to reconstruct time series at unmeasured locations using external variables and training data from measured locations.
